السوداني محي الدين سالم خلال اجتماع وزراء خارجية الكوميسا في هراري هراري 21 أكتوبر 2026 – طالب وزير الخارجية السوداني محي الدين سالم، الأربعاء، بتشكيل آلية أفريقية موحدة لمواجهة المليشيات المتمردة والجماعات الإرهابية. وشارك سالم، مترئسًا وفد السودان، في أعمال الاجتماع الـ21 لوزراء خارجية دول السوق المشتركة للشرق والجنوب الأفريقي “الكوميسا”، المنعقد في العاصمة الزيمبابوية هراري. ودعا محي الدين سالم، خلال حديثه في الاجتماع، إلى تشكيل “آلية إقليمية موحدة للتعامل مع التحديات الأمنية والسياسية، ومواجهة الحركات المتمردة والجماعات الإرهابية العابرة للحدود التي تستغل الأزمات لتهريب السلع والإضرار بالاستقرار الاقتصادي ورفع تكاليف المعيشة”. وطالب بضرورة تكامل جهود دول المنطقة لمكافحة الجريمة المنظمة والاتجار بالمخدرات، والتصدي للمخاطر التي تهدد المجتمعات الأفريقية، خاصة النساء والشباب وكبار السن، في ظل استغلال أوضاع الفقر والهشاشة. وأشار إلى أن استقرار دول المنطقة يمثل شرطًا أساسيًا لنجاح جهود التكامل الاقتصادي، وتعزيز التجارة البينية، وتحقيق الأمن الغذائي، وحماية الحدود. وحث دول الكوميسا على توحيد الرؤى والمواقف إزاء التهديدات المشتركة، بما يعزز قدرة القارة على معالجة أزماتها وتحقيق الاستقرار المستدام. وقال الوزير إن موقف السودان ثابت حيال توصيف قوات الدعم السريع بأنها «مليشيا متمردة» في الأدبيات والمداولات الإقليمية، نظرًا إلى الجرائم والانتهاكات الجسيمة التي ارتكبتها بحق المدنيين، إضافة إلى ما وصفه بالدمار الممنهج للبنية التحتية. ودعا وزراء خارجية دول الكوميسا إلى زيارة العاصمة الخرطوم للوقوف ميدانيًا على حجم الدمار والآثار التي خلفتها اعتداءات قوات الدعم السريع على البلاد ومؤسساتها. ويخوض الجيش السوداني، منذ 15 أبريل 2023، حربًا ضد قوات الدعم السريع، اندلعت في الخرطوم، قبل أن تنحصر بصورة رئيسية في إقليمي كردفان والنيل الأزرق، فيما لا يزال معظم إقليم دارفور تحت سيطرة قوات الدعم السريع. وقالت وزارة الخارجية، في بيان، إن اجتماع الكوميسا أجاز التوصيات الواردة في تقرير حالة السلم والأمن في السودان والمنطقة. وأفادت بأن التوصيات شملت احترام سيادة السودان ووحدة أراضيه واستقلال مؤسساته الوطنية، علاوة على الرفض التام للتدخلات الخارجية والإمدادات العسكرية والمالية للأطراف المسلحة والمليشيات. ودعت التوصيات، بحسب البيان، إلى تنسيق جهود الكوميسا والاتحاد الأفريقي والمبادرات الأفريقية الداعمة للسلام، وتجنب تعارض المسارات التفاوضية. وأوضحت الوزارة أن التوصيات تضمنت دعم الترتيبات الفنية واللوجستية لإعادة افتتاح المقر الدائم لمحكمة العدل التابعة للكوميسا في الخرطوم، إلى جانب حشد المؤسسات التنموية والقطاع الخاص الأفريقي للمساهمة في جهود التعافي وإعادة الإعمار في السودان. الكلمات: إعادة الإعمار في السودان الكوميسا قوات الدعم السريع محي الدين سالم وزارة الخارجية السودانية مقالات ذات صلة اجتماع مشترك بين (السيادي) ووكلاء الوزارات لإجازة موازنة 2026 – أعلنت لجنة المعلمين السودانيين، الأربعاء، دخول معلمي ولاية الخرطوم في إضراب عن العمل، في إطار تصعيد نقابي للمطالبة بحقوق الأساتذة وزيادة الأجور. وسلّمت لجنة المعلمين، في 7 أكتوبر الجاري، مذكرة إلى القصر الجمهوري، دعت فيها إلى رفع الحد الأدنى للأجور إلى 500 ألف جنيه، وإصلاح هيكل الأجور، وصرف المتأخرات والبدلات، وضمان انتظام صرف المرتبات. وقالت اللجنة، في تقرير، إن الإضراب في الخرطوم «نُفذ بصورة قوية في عدد من محليات الولاية، حيث سجلت محليتا كرري وشرق النيل استجابة واسعة للإضراب». وأفادت باستمرار الإضراب غدًا الخميس، كما أشادت بتفهم المجتمع لدوافع الخطوة، ودعت السلطات إلى الاستجابة لمطالب المعلمين، معتبرة أن الإضراب يمثل رسالة احتجاج من فئة تشكل ركيزة أساسية في المجتمع. وكشف المتحدث الرسمي باسم لجنة المعلمين السودانيين، سامي الباقر، عن بلوغ نسبة الإضراب بين المعلمين نحو 90% في مدارس محلية بحري، و95% في محلية أمبدة، فيما تُقدّر بنحو 60% في مرحلتي الأساس والمتوسطة بمحلية شرق النيل. وأوضح الباقر، في تصريح لـ«سودان تربيون»، أن نسبة الإضراب في مدارس مرحلة الأساس بمحلية بحري بلغت 95%، ووصلت إلى 100% في بعض المدارس، بينما شهدت مدارس المرحلة الثانوية تفاوتًا في الاستجابة للإضراب، فيما لم تتجاوز نسبة المعلمين الذين واصلوا العمل 2%. وذكر أن نسبة الإضراب في مدارس محلية أمبدة بلغت 95%، لافتًا إلى أن نسبة حضور المعلمين والطلاب في مدارس المحلية تُقدّر بنحو 20%. وتتمثل مطالب المعلمين في إنهاء التفاوت في الأجور بين الولايات، ومعالجة أوضاع المعلمين في إقليمي دارفور وكردفان، إلى جانب حماية التعليم العام من التراجع، وإلزام الدولة بتحمل مسؤولياتها تجاه التعليم الحكومي. الكلمات: أجور المعلمين إضراب المعلمين الخرطوم رواتب المعلمين لجنة المعلمين السودانيين مقالات ذات صلة والي شمال الإنساني إلى سقوط أكثر من 200 ألف قتيل منذ اندلاع المواجهات في أبريل 2023. وقد تسببت الحرب في تفشي المجاعة في عدة مناطق، بالإضافة إلى موجات نزوح واسعة النطاق داخلياً وخارجياً، مما خلق واحدة من أسوأ المتحدة إلى السودان، على ضرورة أن يكون لدى شركاء السودان الدوليين والإقليميين "التزام راسخ بإنهاء الحرب، وتخفيف معاناة الشعب السوداني، ودعم حقه في مستقبل يسوده السلام والأمن والكرامة في ظل سودان موحد". جاء ذلك خلال الاجتماع التشاوري حول تعزيز تنسيق مبادرات وجهود السلام في السودان، الذي عقد اليوم الأربعاء في مقر الأمم المتحدة بجنيف، بمشاركة ممثلين رفيعي المستوى من 22 دولة، إلى جانب الأمم المتحدة، والاتحاد الأفريقي، والاتحاد الأوروبي، والهيئة الحكومية الدولية المعنية بالتنمية (إيغاد)، وجامعة الدول العربية. يعد هذا الاجتماع السادس من نوعه، ويشكل آلية تنسيقية هامة تجمع الأطراف الدولية والإقليمية المشاركة في جهود حل النزاع في السودان، ولا يضم في مداولاته الحكومة السودانية أو قوات الدعم السريع، رغم أنه يتم التشاور مع أطراف النزاع قبل انعقاده واطلاعهم على نتائجه بعد اختتامه. وقد عقدت الاجتماعات السابقة في القاهرة، وجيبوتي، ونواكشوط، وبروكسل. وفي كلمته الافتتاحية، أكد هافيستو أن أصوات الشعب السوداني يجب أن توجه المداولات، وأن "تطلعاتهم يجب أن تظل المعيار الذي نقيس به مدى تقدمنا". وأوضح أن المناقشات ستتمحور حول جهود خفض التصعيد وبناء الثقة بين الأطراف، ومسار الانتقال نحو مرحلة سياسية انتقالية وعملية سياسية يقودها السودانيون، بالإضافة إلى الأبعاد الإقليمية للنزاع وكيفية منع تدهور الأوضاع وامتداد النزاع بشكل أكبر إلى الدول المجاورة. وأشار هافيستو إلى أن قيمة هذا الاجتماع تعتمد على قدرة المشاركين على تحويل الإدراك المشترك لمدى ضرورة التحرك العاجل إلى إجراءات عملية، قائلا: "نحن مدينون للشعب السوداني باهتمام مستمر، وانخراط متسق، وعمل حازم. ومع اقتراب شهر نيسان/أبريل 2027، يجب علينا بذل كل ما في وسعنا لضمان أن يشكل هذا التاريخ نقطة تحول نحو السلام، بدلا من أن يكون بداية لعام آخر من الحرب والمعاناة. إن هدفنا من هذا الاجتماع هو تسخير جهودنا الجماعية لخدمة الشعب السوداني". لا أحد بمنأى عن التبعات من جانبه، قال ألكسندر فاسيل، وزير الدولة السويسري للشؤون الخارجية، إنه بعد مرور 1285 يوما على الحرب في السودان، أصبحت اليوم "بالغة التعقيد وأكثر فتكا بكثير"، حيث تشهد البلاد واحدة من أسوأ الأزمات الإنسانية وأزمات الحماية في العالم. وأكد فاسيل أن سويسرا، التي شاركت في استضافة الاجتماع، ترى أن عملية السلام في السودان لن تنجح إلا إذا تضافرت المسارات الأمنية والسياسية والإنسانية. وفي حين يمثل السودان أكبر استجابة إنسانية لسويسرا في أفريقيا، فإن بلاده تواصل دورها كـ "جسر للتواصل وميسر للحوار"، حيث تجمع أطرافا سودانية في إطار غير رسمي للمساعدة في تهيئة الأرضية للمفاوضات السياسية الرسمية، بحسب الوزير السويسري. إلا أن فاسيل شدد على أن حماية المدنيين وتوفير الوصول الإنساني لا ينبغي أن ينتظرا التوصل إلى وقف إطلاق نار أو حل سياسي، وأضاف: "يعاني المدنيون وهم يفقدون حياتهم اليوم. لذا يجب على أطراف النزاع حمايتهم في جميع الأوقات وتحت أي ظرف، وتسهيل وصولهم إلى المساعدات الإنسانية". وفيما أقر بأن المشاركين في الاجتماع قد لا يتبنون وجهات نظر متطابقة حول ديناميكيات الوضع في السودان، إلا أنه رأى أن هناك اتفاقا عاما على عدم وجود حل عسكري للنزاع، وأن السبيل الوحيد لإنهائه بشكل دائم يكمن في دعم حوار شامل يقوده السودانيون أنفسهم. وقال في هذا الصدد: "لن يكون أي وفد في هذه القاعة بمنأى عن تبعات سودان ممزق يعاني من عنف ممتد كالذي نشهده حاليا. لذا، أدعو الجميع هنا إلى التحلي بالشجاعة والاتفاق على تكثيف جهودنا الجماعية". ♦ تحميل تطبيق أخبار الأمم المتحدة بالعربية من متجر آبل لأجهزة الأيفون والآيباد IOS أو من متجر غوغل لأجهزة أندرويد Android . ♦ الاشتراك في لجنة المعلمين تكشف عن تنفيذ الإضراب بنسبة كبيرة في الخرطوم 21 أكتوبر، 2026 1:19 م إضراب المعلمين في الخرطوم -21 أكتوبر 2026- إعلام لجنة المعلمين الخرطوم – 21 أكتوبر 2026 – راديو دبنقا أعلنت لجنة المعلمين السودانيين عن بدء تنفيذ إضراب المعلمين المعلن في ولاية الخرطوم، اليوم الأربعاء، على أن يستمر يوم غدٍ الخميس. وأكدت اللجنة، في بيان لها، أن الإضراب نُفِّذ بنسب عالية جداً في كل محليات ولاية الخرطوم، وخاصة محلية كرري التي شهدت استجابة قوية وبنسبة مرتفعة، وكذلك في محلية شرق النيل. وأوضحت أن الإضراب سيتواصل غداً في يومه الثاني، على أن تجتمع اللجنة العليا للإضراب يوم السبت القادم لتقييم الموقف وإصدار القرارات اللازمة للأسبوع المقبل. وقال سامي الباقر، الناطق باسم لجنة المعلمين، لـ “راديو دبنقا”، إن الإضراب يأتي في إطار المطالبة برفع الحد الأدنى للأجور من 12 ألف جنيه إلى 500 ألف جنيه، وإصلاح الهيكل الراتبي بما يتناسب مع تكاليف المعيشة، وصرف جميع المتأخرات والبدلات والاستحقاقات المالية للمعلمين والعاملين بالتعليم في كل الولايات دون استثناء، وضمان انتظام صرف المرتبات في موعد أقصاه اليوم الخامس من كل شهر، وتحقيق العدالة في الأجور والاستحقاقات بين الولايات. وأكد تمسك اللجنة بضرورة تخصيص 20% من الموازنة العامة للتعليم العام، وتمويل التعليم الحكومي، ومركزة مرتبات العاملين به؛ حتى لا يظل المعلم رهينةً لعجز الولايات وتفاوت مواردها، وحتى لا تتحول المدارس الحكومية إلى مؤسسات عاجزة عن أداء رسالتها، بما يفتح الطريق أمام توسع التعليم الخاص على حساب حق أبناء الشعب في التعليم. تضامن نقابي من جانبها، أعلنت أجسام نقابية ومهنية – من بينها تنسيقية المهنيين والنقابات السودانية، ولجنة المعلمين، ونقابة الصحفيين السودانيين، وتجمع البيئيين السودانيين – عن تضامنها مع المعلمين في إضرابهم. وطالبت تنسيقية المهنيين والنقابات السودانية الجهات المعنية بالاستجابة الجادة والفورية للمطالب المطروحة، ومعالجة أزمة الأجور والاستحقاقات المالية، ووضع معالجات عملية ومستدامة لأوضاع العاملين في قطاع التعليم. كما أكدت التنسيقية ضرورة احترام الحقوق والحريات النقابية، وحماية المعلمين والمعلمات من أي إجراءات تعسفية بسبب مشاركتهم في العمل النقابي السلمي أو مطالبتهم بحقوقهم المشروعة. ودعت جميع النقابات والأجسام المهنية والعمالية إلى توحيد الجهود والتضامن مع المعلمين والمعلمات، باعتبار أن الدفاع عن حقوقهم جزء لا يتجزأ من معركة استعادة الحقوق المهنية والعمالية في السودان. وحذّرت التنسيقية من استمرار تجاهل أزمة التعليم، مؤكدةً أن التعليم ليس خدمة هامشية يمكن تأجيلها، وأن المعلم ليس عاملاً يمكن مطالبته بأداء رسالته في ظل الجوع وانعدام الاستقرار وغياب الحد الأدنى من مقومات الحياة. ethiopia.title: Supreme Audit Institutions Deliberating On Strengthening Collaboration, Accountability in Africa
ethiopia.content: Africa: Supreme Audit Institutions Deliberating On Strengthening Collaboration, Accountability in Africa - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: Supreme Audit Institutions Deliberating On Strengthening Collaboration, Accountability in Africa 20 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — A workshop aimed at strengthening collaboration and improving the effectiveness and sustainability of public-sector auditing across Africa is underway in Addis Ababa. Opening the three-day capacity development workshop today, Ethiopia's Auditor General Meseret Damtie said strengthening African Supreme Audit Institutions (SAIs) is essential in order to promote accountable governance, sound public financial management and sustainable development across the continent. She emphasized that improved audit quality, institutional capacity and collaboration are essential to enable audit institutions fulfil their mandates effectively. "At the heart of ARISE (African Regional Initiative for Strengthening Effectiveness) is the spirit of peer support and collaboration," the Auditor General said, highlighting the importance of cooperation among participating institutions, programme coordinators, peer SAIs and development partners in achieving sustainable results. Meseret linked the principles of cooperation and collective responsibility underpinning ARISE to Ethiopia's Medemer philosophy, which emphasizes synergy, shared contributions and common goals. She highlighted the importance of collaboration in strengthening institutions and advancing sustainable development, reflecting the program's emphasis on partnerships and collective efforts to improve public-sector accountability across Africa. INTOSAI Development Initiative (IDI) representative, Muhammed Dabo, stressed that sustainable improvements in Supreme Audit Institutions require more than technical training, emphasizing strong institutional systems, effective leadership, capable personnel and the ability to manage change. "Each partner has a distinct role, but we share one objective: stronger, more effective and sustainable Supreme Audit Institutions," he said, underscoring the complementary roles of beneficiary SAIs, peer institutions, regional organizations and development partners. Dabo encouraged the participants to share experiences openly, identify challenges early, adapt when necessary and develop practical solutions for their respective institutions. He stressed that the workshop's success should be measured by the lessons applied and improvements achieved after participants return to their work. ethiopia.title: TPLF Had Been Preparing for War - PM Abiy
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: TPLF Had Been Preparing for War - PM Abiy - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: TPLF Had Been Preparing for War - PM Abiy 20 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — The defunct TPLF had been preparing for another round of war, violating the Pretoria Agreement, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed revealed. During an interview with the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC), he said the TPLF violated the Pretoria Agreement signed in October 2022. The PM recalled that the key elements of the Pretoria Agreement included cessation of hostilities, restoration of all services, disarmament, return of displaced people, and recognition of the constitutional order. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The federal government had fulfilled everything that was possible and expected of it, he added. On the contrary, the TPLF had been purchasing and soliciting weapons as well as openly recruiting young people instead of implementing the agreement to disarm combatants. Above all, PM Abiy pointed out that after the agreement, the TPLF used displaced persons as hostages to prevent them from returning to their homes. Additionally, it engaged in destroying and closing down infrastructure--including airlines, banking, and telecommunications--that had been restored by the Federal Government to deliver services. Despite the group's misdeeds, the PM stated that the government had forewarned that war was not worthwhile and that peace was preferable. However, the TPLF disregarded the advice and collaborated with various forces, and violated the Pretoria Agreement by initiating an unnecessary war. Immense damage has been inflicted on the public as a result of the war instigated by the TPLF, he noted. War is bad and yields no benefit, the Premier further noted, adding that a war fought for the interests of foreign forces is even worse. The psychological damage is not to be taken lightly and damage has also been inflicted on development and the economy. PM Abiy stressed that young people carrying Kalashnikovs should therefore return to work and participate in the development and rehabilitation of Tigray. Noting that many young people were forcibly recruited, he advised those who have not yet returned to return to normal life. He stated that the leaders of the TPLF have been declaring war for 50 years without dying or being wounded themselves; instead they sent their children and families abroad and to Addis Ababa where they are engaged in business and construction. Through the spirit of Medemer, Ethiopia and Kenya must continue building on our existing cooperation in clean energy, connectivity, telecommunications, and trade to create greater opportunities and shared prosperity for our people," he said. The two countries also cooperate in regional security, cross-border infrastructure, trade, telecommunications, and electricity interconnections, supporting economic integration and development across the Horn of Africa, it was learned. Taye underscored the importance of reliable statistics in driving evidence-based development in Africa. Addressing the opening of the 10th Session of the Statistical Commission for Africa and the 12th Meeting of the Regional Committee of the United Nations Global Geospatial Information Management for Africa in Addis Ababa, the President said Ethiopia's development planning is anchored in measurable targets and reliable data. He emphasized that development cannot be effectively planned, sustained, or scaled up without accurate measurement, noting that official statistics are essential for shaping development strategies, tracking progress, and strengthening accountability. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The President also highlighted Ethiopia's reforms in the financial and digital sectors, including the National Digital Payment Strategy, financial sector liberalization, interoperable payment infrastructure, and the national digital identification program, Fayda. He said Fayda enables secure electronic verification and expands access to banking, mobile money, telecommunications, and other essential public services, demonstrating how digital infrastructure can improve service delivery and financial inclusion. According to the President, mobile money and mobile banking accounts in Ethiopia reached 257 million and processed more than 24 trillion birr in transactions during the first nine months of 2026, reflecting the expansion of the country's financial and digital systems. Drawing lessons from these reforms, he stressed that statistics must serve as practical tools for sustainable development and be communicated clearly and accessibly to policymakers and citizens, rather than being treated as an end in themselves. He also called for statistical institutions to integrate and safeguard diverse data sources without compromising statistical integrity, emphasizing that innovation must reinforce data quality, institutional independence, and public trust. The President urged African governments to protect the professional independence of official statistics, strengthen legal and institutional frameworks, invest in national statistical systems, and ground policy decisions in scientific evidence. He cautioned that poor-quality data undermines evidence-based policymaking, impedes development, and weakens accountability. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: News - Funding Shortfalls Threaten Health Services in Ethiopia's Conflict-Hit Regions, UN Warns - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: News - Funding Shortfalls Threaten Health Services in Ethiopia's Conflict-Hit Regions, UN Warns 21 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Funding shortages threaten essential health and nutrition services in Ethiopia's conflict-affected regions, with 10 of the 16 operational mobile health and nutrition teams in Amhara expected to shut down by the end of October, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said. According to OCHA , only 16 of the 57 mobile health and nutrition teams required in Amhara are currently operational. Of these, 10 are expected to cease operations by the end of the month because of funding constraints. Humanitarian partners are continuing to deliver life-saving assistance despite insecurity and access challenges in parts of northern Ethiopia, including Tigray, Amhara and Afar, the UN agency said. In Tigray, additional medical, nutrition and other essential supplies have reached communities and health facilities, with further deliveries expected. Humanitarian partners are also working with regional authorities to facilitate access and expand assistance. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines On Tuesday, Humanitarian Coordinator in Ethiopia Ozonnia Ojielo met officials from the newly established caretaker interim administration in Tigray, emphasizing the need for unhindered humanitarian access, according to OCHA. In Amhara, humanitarian partners are preparing to provide food assistance to approximately 100,000 people in Wag Hamra and North Wollo zones. Operations are also continuing in Afar, although limited funding remains a major obstacle to expanding the response. OCHA said humanitarian needs across Ethiopia continue to exceed available resources, warning that funding shortfalls are undermining efforts to sustain essential services for vulnerable communities. The agency reiterated its call for all parties to facilitate the expansion of life-saving humanitarian assistance and ensure humanitarian actors can reach people in need. The funding shortfall extends beyond health services, affecting food assistance, refugee protection and support for internally displaced people (IDPs), as previously reported by Addis Standard. Earlier this month, Addis Standard reported that IDPs in camps in Debre Birhan were facing worsening shortages of food, medicines, healthcare and other essential services as humanitarian organizations scaled back or withdrew operations amid funding constraints. Continued displacement from conflict-affected areas has further strained already limited resources. The situation reflects a broader displacement crisis across Amhara. As of early 2025, more than 660,000 people were estimated to be living in 31 IDP sites and collective centres across seven administrative zones, with North and South Wollo accounting for approximately 55% of the sites. Major displacement locations include the Bakelo and China camps in Debre Birhan and the Jara IDP Centre in North Wollo. ethiopia.title: Eritrea Tells Us There Is No 'Crisis' Between Ethiopia and Eritrea
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Eritrea Tells Us There Is No 'Crisis' Between Ethiopia and Eritrea - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Eritrea Tells Us There Is No 'Crisis' Between Ethiopia and Eritrea 21 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Eritrea's Ambassador to the United Nations, Sophia Tesfamariam, has told senior US diplomats that there is no "crisis" between Ethiopia and Eritrea, while urging Washington and other international actors to address what she described as threats to Eritrea's sovereignty and territorial integrity. In a statement posted on X on 20 October, Sophia said she held "constructive engagements" with Mike Waltz, the US permanent representative to the UN, and Jeffrey Bartos, the US representative to the UN for Management and Reform, to discuss developments in the Horn of Africa and present Asmara's position on the region's deteriorating security situation. Over the last two weeks, the two countries exchanged accusations at the United Nations over their deteriorating relations. Ethiopia sent a letter to the UN Security Council in early October accusing Eritrean forces of an "all-out invasion" of parts of Tigray in northern Ethiopia and invoking its right to self-defence. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Eritrea rejected Ethiopia's account and, in its own communication to the Council, accused Addis Abeba of threatening a war of aggression over Red Sea access. The two governments' competing accounts have emerged alongside renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia and heightened fears of a broader regional conflict. Sophia said she had "reiterated that there is no 'crisis' between Eritrea and Ethiopia" and argued that the international community should pay closer attention to developments within Ethiopia. She urged Addis Abeba to "respect Eritrea's sovereign territories and stop diverting attention from its domestic issues." The ambassador also accused Ethiopia of pursuing a three-year campaign concerning access to the Red Sea and making continued threats against Eritrea's sovereignty, including what she described as threats to annex Eritrean territory. She called on countries with influence in the region to act "responsibly and proactively" to prevent a wider conflict, cautioning them against making statements that could embolden Ethiopia's leadership. "Eritrea's sovereignty and territorial integrity must be respected," she said, adding that preventing renewed conflict requires addressing underlying threats, upholding international law and acting before tensions escalate. Credit: Office of the Prime Minister of Ethiopia Diplomatic tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea remain unresolved despite international appeals for restraint, with the neighboring countries continuing to exchange accusations over territorial security, armed opposition groups and access to the Red Sea. The confrontation has intensified following Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s October 19 warning that Eritrea could face severe consequences if it continued providing support to groups opposing his government. In a Tigrigna-language interview broadcast by Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC), Abiy accused Eritrea of allowing its territory to serve as a base for forces hostile to Ethiopia while maintaining that peaceful cooperation remained possible. The remarks, detailed in Kulu Media’s report on Abiy’s warning , came amid renewed military operations in Tigray and heightened concern over the possibility of a wider regional confrontation. Eritrea has rejected Ethiopian accusations of supporting armed opposition groups. Asmara has instead accused Addis Ababa of threatening its sovereignty through demands for greater access to the Red Sea. International Pressure for De-escalation The United States and United Kingdom have urged both governments to avoid further escalation and resolve their differences through diplomacy. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called for restraint during discussions with Abiy Ahmed, emphasizing respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity. The United Kingdom subsequently urged renewed diplomatic engagement and expressed support for African Union efforts to reduce tensions. As detailed in Kulu Media’s coverage of the UK’s diplomatic appeal , London also warned about the humanitarian consequences of renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia. The Associated Press reported that international concerns have increased as renewed fighting in Tigray places additional pressure on the fragile security arrangements established after the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement. Competing Claims Over Border Security Ethiopia has accused Eritrean forces of entering its territory and supporting insurgent groups, allegations Eritrea disputes. Earlier this month, Ethiopia informed the United Nations Security Council that it was invoking its right to self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter. Eritrea rejected that justification and accused Ethiopia of threatening its territorial integrity. The Associated Press reported that the competing allegations could not be independently verified in full. The confrontation has also been complicated by Ethiopia’s longstanding interest in securing reliable maritime access, including through arrangements involving Red Sea ports. Eritrea regards any attempt to obtain sovereign control over its territory as a threat to national sovereignty. Despite repeated international calls for dialogue, there has been no independently confirmed agreement on a new ceasefire, military withdrawal or formal bilateral negotiation process. The absence of such an agreement leaves the relationship vulnerable to further deterioration as military and political developments continue in northern Ethiopia. The American envoy proposed discussions involving technical experts from the three countries to address outstanding issues in a potential settlement. He also presented documents outlining Washington’s approach to ending the conflict. The discussions followed Witkoff’s meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European representatives in Oslo on Tuesday, where participants examined proposals covering security guarantees, energy infrastructure and possible arrangements for a ceasefire. According to Associated Press , the latest diplomatic initiative seeks to revive negotiations that have struggled to produce a breakthrough despite repeated international efforts. Russia Signals Interest in Renewed US Relations Putin thanked US President Donald Trump for his efforts to negotiate an end to the conflict and expressed Russia’s interest in restoring economic relations with Washington, according to the Russian news agencies. The Kremlin also indicated its willingness to discuss wider international issues, including tensions involving Iran. The meeting took place amid concerns among Ukrainian officials and European allies about the direction of US policy toward Russia and the terms of a potential peace agreement. Although Witkoff expressed optimism about the possibility of renewed negotiations, Russia has not publicly accepted a new ceasefire framework or confirmed a date for trilateral talks. Prisoner Release Accompanies Diplomatic Talks The diplomatic meeting coincided with Russia’s release of American citizen Stephen Hubbard, who had been imprisoned after being accused of fighting alongside Ukrainian forces. Hubbard, a former teacher from Michigan, had been detained since 2022 and was sentenced in 2024 to nearly seven years in prison. The United States previously designated him as wrongfully detained. The diplomatic initiative also follows uncertainty over American military assistance, including a temporary interruption in intelligence sharing with Ukraine that was resolved earlier this month. According to Associated Press , President Trump had personally requested Hubbard’s release. The White House said the arrangement did not require the United States to release another prisoner in exchange. The release represented a concrete diplomatic gesture during the renewed engagement between Washington and Moscow, although it did not establish progress toward a broader settlement of the war. Fighting Continues Despite Diplomatic Efforts The latest negotiations come as Russian and Ukrainian forces continue military operations, including drone and missile attacks affecting civilian areas and energy infrastructure. Ukrainian authorities reported additional casualties and damage from overnight Russian strikes on October 21, underscoring the continuing humanitarian consequences of the conflict. Ukraine has repeatedly emphasized that any lasting settlement must include credible security guarantees and protect its sovereignty. Russia and Ukraine remain divided over territorial control and the conditions necessary for ending hostilities, making a comprehensive agreement difficult despite renewed American mediation. The latest meeting has reopened discussions about a possible ceasefire, but significant questions remain over whether Moscow and Kyiv can agree on its terms. For now, the proposed resumption of trilateral negotiations represents a diplomatic opportunity rather than a confirmed breakthrough in efforts to end the war. Continue Reading Diplomacy Abiy Ahmed Warns Eritrea of Severe Consequences Over Alleged Rebel Support Ethiopian prime minister warns Eritrea against supporting armed opposition groups. Published 1 day ago on October 20, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed speaks during an EBC interview on October 19, 2026, in which he warned Eritrea over alleged support for armed opposition groups. Image Credit: EBC / Screenshot by Kulu Media Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has warned Eritrea of severe consequences if it continues to support armed groups opposing his government, delivering one of his clearest public warnings to the neighboring country amid renewed fighting in Tigray and growing fears of a wider regional conflict. Speaking in a Tigrigna-language interview broadcast by the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC) on Monday, October 19, Abiy accused Eritrea of allowing its territory to be used by groups hostile to Ethiopia. The prime minister said cooperation between the two countries would offer greater benefits than confrontation and warned against ignoring Ethiopia’s appeals. According to Interview , Abiy said Eritrea’s continued role as a base for Ethiopia’s adversaries would bring severe consequences. The warning marks a further escalation in rhetoric between Addis Ababa and Asmara, which severed diplomatic relations earlier this month following competing allegations of military aggression and interference in each other’s internal affairs. Ethiopia has repeatedly accused Eritrea of supporting the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and other armed opposition groups. Eritrea has rejected accusations that it is backing Ethiopian rebels and has accused Addis Ababa of pursuing hostile policies toward its sovereignty. Warning Comes Amid Renewed Tigray Conflict Abiy’s remarks followed weeks of military operations in Tigray, where Ethiopian federal forces and allied Tigray Peace Force (TPF) fighters have regained control of several major towns previously held by TPLF-aligned forces. The military developments have brought Ethiopian government forces closer to Eritrea’s border, intensifying concerns that the confrontation could expand beyond Tigray. As documented in Kulu Media’s coverage of the border tensions , troop movements, disputed territorial claims and the collapse of diplomatic relations have increased the risk of direct confrontation between the two countries. Earlier in October, Ethiopia accused Eritrean troops of crossing into its territory and occupying parts of northern Tigray. The Ethiopian government subsequently invoked Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, asserting its right to self-defense. Eritrea, meanwhile, called for UN action against Ethiopia, accusing Addis Ababa of preparing military aggression. The competing accusations have not been independently established in full. Abiy Says TPLF Is Nearing Its End During the interview, Abiy also addressed the TPLF’s declining control over major towns in Tigray following the latest federal military offensive. He suggested that the organization was approaching the end of its political dominance and pledged development across the region. His comments came days after the federal government established a caretaker administration with a six-month mandate to restore public services, improve security and prepare for regional elections. The TPLF-aligned leadership has rejected the new administration, challenging its legitimacy and the authority of its decisions. Abiy urged Tigray residents to preserve unity and public institutions while preparations for a future elected administration continue. Despite the federal government’s territorial gains, the security situation remains uncertain in some parts of Tigray, and political disagreements over the region’s future remain unresolved. Ethiopia and Eritrea Remain on Opposing Diplomatic Paths Relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have deteriorated sharply since the two countries restored diplomatic ties in 2018. The former allies fought together against the TPLF during the 2020–2022 Tigray war, but their relationship subsequently worsened over regional security, the Pretoria peace agreement and Ethiopia’s ambitions for greater access to the Red Sea. Abiy’s latest remarks combined a warning against alleged Eritrean interference with an appeal for peaceful cooperation. He said good neighborly relations and partnership remained the appropriate path forward. International concern has also increased. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently warned of wider war and urged restraint as military tensions continued along the border. Abiy’s October 19 warning does not amount to a formal declaration of war or an announcement of a new military offensive against Eritrea. However, the direct warning from Ethiopia’s prime minister adds another layer of political tension to an already volatile confrontation, with renewed fighting in Tigray threatening to destabilize the wider Horn of Africa. ethiopia.content: The El-Alamein Quadrilateral and the Risks of Geopolitical Polarization in the North East Africa – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-21 The El-Alamein Quadrilateral and the Risks of Geopolitical Polarization in the North East Africa 0 Comments The rapid changes that are taking place in the North East Africa region shake the very foundation of the post-1991 geopolitical arrangement imposed on the Horn of Africa, Nile Basin and Red Sea. Ethiopia’s civilizational, cultural and national resilience is reshaping the regional geo-economic map linking the Nile Basin, Horn of Africa and Red Sea into one strategic theater. The operationalization of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam Nile (GERD) rewrites the geopolitical mathematics of the Nile with reason and fairness. Ethiopia’s emergence as a geo-economic game-changer in the geo-economically dormant terrain of the region activates the countries to utilize the waters of the Nile for their prosperity. South Sudan seeing this trend is intending to construct the Fula Dam to power its economy and safeguard its water security. Ethiopia, questioning the legitimacy of past decisions that deprived her of access to the sea, facing chokepoint wars, and anticipating maritime blockades, goes on striving for a durable access to the sea through a reasonable and fair manner. The new breed of leadership seeks to peacefully and legally redress the 1991 injustice that makes Ethiopia landlocked. This illegitimate act was undertaken by the late Egyptian Secretary-General of the UN Boutros Boutros-Ghali in league with the TPLF-Ethiopia and PFDJ-Eritrea. The strategic sea changes in the region re-graphing the “geo” of the Nile and Red Sea disputes Egypt’s regional vision built on absolute security architecture. The fundamental change in the basic structures of the regional system has forced Egyptian officials to stop the geopolitical rebalancing of the Horn. Egypt’s Foreign Minister authoring a commentary on News24 in 2025 underlined that Egypt is using its defense and diplomatic machinery to restore its dominium on the “two of the most important axes of Egyptian national security”—Nile Basin and Red Sea. Egypt’s militaristic and diplomatic posture took shape in October 2026 in El-Alamein, forming a Quadrilateral Security Grouping that includes PFDJ-Eritrea, SAF-Sudan and Hassan Sheikh-Somalia. The grouping seeks to re-configure the complicated waters of the Nile and Red Sea without Ethiopia. Egypt which is the brain behind this unilateral governance enterprise chariots the grouping to run the sovereignty of PFDJ-Eritrea, SAF-Sudan and Hassan Sheik-Somalia through Cairo. For Ethiopia, the significance of this assemblage lies not simply in the number of participating states, but in the implications of their emerging military and intelligence coordination for the region’s wider security architecture. The grouping defines Ethiopia as a structural challenger to the alliance and Egypt’s primacy in the region. The emerging security alliance advances Egypt’s Ethiopia strategy which is designed to exploit internal political differences through exporting instabilities. PFJD-Eritrea serves as a liaison in this project. The grouping seeks to promote the dismemberment scenario gaining meaning in the form of Tsimido materially steered by Egypt and PFDJ-Eritrea. This scenario seeking to embroil Ethiopia in “forever wars” intends to control the headwaters of Abay (Blue Nile) and decouple Addis Ababa from the Red Sea. This scenario is being countered by Ethiopia. Ethiopia’s military success, confusing the El-Alamein grouping and surprising the international commentariat, shows Ethiopia cannot be treated as a challenge to be contained but as a concrete pillar of the regional order built on indivisible security paired with open economic architecture. Besides the continued military and intelligence support, the El-Alamein grouping now turns to a full-fledged ideational war against Ethiopia in the global battle for hearts and minds. Egypt and PFJD-Eritrea are now engaged in diplomatic overdrive hell-bent on delegitimizing Ethiopia’s credibility and producing misinformation that materially disadvantage Ethiopia. The regime in Asmara depicts Ethiopia’s measured self-defense as an attempt to control PFDJ-Eritrea’s ports, turn Asmara into an Ethiopian coastal state, and make Addis Ababa a rule maker in the management of the Red Sea. Ethiopia’s peaceful search for sea access is sold by PFDJ-Eritrea and Egypt to the global audience as expansionism, controlling ports and revising the borders of the Horn. This is a scheme to cover up Eritrean incursion and El-Alamein grouping’s support to insurgent groups in Ethiopia. Besides delegitimizing Ethiopia’s reputation, this diplomatic smear campaign organized and directed by El-Alamein bloc is intended to contain Ethiopia as a “landlocked, truncated, weak and circumscribed country.” The El Alamein bloc entails that Egypt seeks to build its Red Sea position on keeping littoral states and non-littoral states apart in order to remake the geography and governance of the Red Sea without Ethiopia. For this to happen, Egypt does so by employing a combination of foreign-policy perceptions, economic pull, security coordination, and military support in the region. The framing of Red Sea for Red Sea littoral states advances closed regionalism and governance unilateralism, embracing Egypt’s conception of Arab Lake. The littoral-centric framing, originated with the formation of the Red Sea Council in 2020, evidently demonstrates the El-Alamein grouping’s policy to exclusively dictate the terms and rules of engagement on all issues of the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. This exclusively competitive approach risks producing overlapping security initiatives, diplomatic polarization and uncertainty for trade and investment in the broader region. The ultimate strategic goal of the El-Alamein grouping is all about undermining the peaceful restoration of Ethiopia’s legitimate access to its natural seashores by PFDJ/TPLF assisted by Egypt together with international complicity. That amounts to omitting Ethiopia’s historicity and ontology on the Red Sea. Professor Tecola Hagos captures this grim reality facing the Horn: “With Ethiopia landlocked, the long-term strategy for the Horn is terribly flawed.” With Ethiopia delinked from the Red Sea and barred from the governance of the water strip, the broader Red Sea and Gulf of Aden connected to the Middle East conflict has become a site of contest where land-based powers set to challenge the sea powers and an arena of zero-sum competition. The international community again sticks to the vocabulary and grammar of de-escalation regarding the tensions surrounding Ethiopia and PFDJ-Eritrea. PFDJ-Eritrea’s aversion to talking over fighting which seeks to profit from a contained, landlocked Ethiopia continues to bring insecurity and underdevelopment. Sadly, that war-footing behavior of PFDJ-Eritrea has brought, according to Hassan Umer Abdalla, “a sort of unconsumed divorce and impossible neighborliness” between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Partners with influence should not lose sight of the Eritrean problem fueled by Egypt’s hegemonic ambitions and turbocharged by rival regional security groupings, including, El-Alamein Quadrilateral Security bloc, that intend to corner and stop Ethiopia from ascending. The El-Alamein security arrangement cannot contribute to stability in the region as it is non-transparent, exclusive and negatively directed towards containing Ethiopia’s development. It has already become a source of mistrust Ethiopia perceives it as an instrument for constraining its legitimate national interests. The international partners plunging themselves in the content while leaving the terms of the conversation that trouble the Nile, Horn and Red Sea overlook the regional security logic—logic of dismemberment. The main objective of regional security architecture underpinned by this logic minted by Egypt is all about safeguarding the singular water, maritime and strategic interests against an existential threat from Ethiopia. Although Ethiopia as a resilient civilizational state has turned this logic of dismemberment into a myth, the same logic poses dangers to the security of the Nile and Horn while fueling the already contested wider Red Sea. The moment demands that the Horn of Africa finally break with the regressive regional architecture of “rules by few” and exclusion that continues to constrain and suffocate the future of the region with zero-sum rivalry and bloc politics. It demands that the Horn of Africa embrace tougher, harder, but more enabling paradigm of “rules through dialogue” and institutional inclusion replacing “rules by few” and unilateral governance. This enabling paradigm ensures that regional cooperation does not become a framework for strategic exclusion, opening new possibilities for the countries of the Horn to consult on and shape an open, inclusive regional architecture of mutual enablement that frames security as a shared responsibility and development as a shared empowerment. For this to happen, a new way of imagining agency, doing politics and exercising power is required by the region to deploy native intelligence and negotiate as a collective with the extended neighborhood—broader Arabian Peninsula—and the wider international community to seize the moment. As the global rules are being re-written in the fraying international order for survival and influence, will the Horn of Africa imagine, think and act otherwise to be an author of its future? This grouping seeks to counter Ethiopia's rising influence, particularly following the operationalization of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), which Ethiopia views as a means to secure its water rights. Ethiopia was one of the world's prominent civilizations in international trade and diplomacy due to its secured sovereign sea access and ports. However, the country had lost its natural, historical, and legal resources due to internal and external political conspiracies as well as various historical circumstances. Efforts being made by the government to address the issue through peaceful and diplomatic means are also showing promising results. The international community has also given due support and attention to Ethiopia's fair demand. In an exclusive interview with ENA, Logistics Researcher Temesgen Walelign said access to the sea plays a significant role in strengthening commercial activities, cargo transport, and global market integration countries. As a result, Ethiopia's lack of port has been incurring additional logistics costs and burdens, preventing products from reaching the global market on time and at competitive prices, he explained. These extra costs affect not only export trade but also cause price hikes on imported goods, ultimately impacting consumers, the researcher added. Moreover, Ethiopia's claim for sea access is appropriate taking into consideration the historical, legal, and long-term development ambitions of the country beyond it geographical location and population. He also praised Ethiopia's efforts in working with neighboring countries to achieve this demand by adhering to principles of give-and-take, peaceful diplomacy, and mutual benefit. Beyond strengthening Ethiopia's commercial and economic capacity, this contributes significantly to fostering lasting regional peace and economic cooperation, Temesgen underscored. Overall, he emphasized that the demand goes beyond current economic needs and forms the foundation of the country's future strategic survival. For his part, the economist Nemomsa Mengesha said Ethiopia's quest for sovereign seaport plays a crucial role in boosting economic competitiveness. More than 100 delegates from Uganda are attending alongside 146 Somali representatives. The gathering includes a review of previous agreements, a business forum and a joint exhibition. The meeting follows the inaugural session of the Somalia–Uganda Joint Permanent Commission, held in Kampala on 7–8 October 2025. Delegations are now assessing progress on earlier commitments and identifying challenges affecting their implementation. Ongoing discussions cover security, defence, labour, health, energy, fisheries, finance, transport, civil aviation, tourism, product standards and statistics. A bilateral labour agreement is among the proposed documents scheduled for signing, alongside other agreements concerning air services, military training, customs, health and statistics. It has not yet been confirmed which agreements have been formally signed. Related articles Somalia, Uganda Agree on Free Visas on Arrival for Diplomatic and Service Passport Holders El Niño: WMO, OCHA Call for Urgent Action to Protect People Most at Risk The business forum is also showcasing investment and trade opportunities, with presentations scheduled from Uganda Airlines, SOMINVEST and investment promotion institutions. Uganda has long supported Somalia in the security sector, while both countries are also members of the East African Community (EAC), which Somalia joined in 2024. According to the official programme, discussions will continue on 22 October, when delegates are scheduled to endorse agreed outcomes and sign the Mogadishu Declaration on bilateral investment and trade cooperation. The agreement was signed on Tuesday in Wuhu, the city in China's Anhui province where Chery is based, between Chery Overseas Investment Corp. and Dahabshiil Motors, the group's vehicle unit. It makes Dahabshiil Motors an authorized Chery dealer in Somalia and includes warranty coverage for buyers, the Somali Embassy in China said in a statement announcing the deal. Hodan Osman Abdi, Somalia's ambassador to China, attended the signing and congratulated both companies. The embassy said the partnership would give Somali consumers access to Chery vehicles backed by warranty services and would strengthen commercial ties between Somali businesses and Chinese manufacturers. The terms of the deal and the Chery models that will be offered were not disclosed. A growing car business Dahabshiil Motors was set up in 2019, when it brought Hyundai to Somaliland as the South Korean carmaker's sole distributor in the Somali regions. It opened with eight Hyundai models, including the Santa Fe, Tucson, Creta and Elantra, along with a commercial bus and a light truck, and built repair and service workshops to support them. Buyers could pay in cash or take Islamic murabaha financing from the group's bank. The unit, which operates in Somaliland and Somalia, has since added Toyota, BYD, JMC and Sinotruk to its range and now sells new vehicles, spare parts, servicing and financing. Chery is its fourth Chinese brand, after BYD, JMC and Sinotruk. Chery, founded in 1997, sold 2.81 million vehicles in 2025 and exported 1.34 million of them, up 17.4% from a year earlier. The company says it has been China's top exporter of passenger vehicles for 23 years in a row. Call for a local plant Abdi used the signing to press Chery to consider building a vehicle plant in Somalia. She pointed to the country's location on the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, its ports and its membership of the East African Community, the regional trade bloc Somalia joined in 2024. She said such an investment could create jobs and build technical skills among young Somalis. The embassy said it would keep working to expand trade and investment between Somalia and China and to help Somali companies gain access to the Chinese market. From remittances to fuel and phones Dahabshiil began in 1970 as a small trading business in Burao, in what is now Somaliland, founded by Duale's father, Mohamed Said Duale. It grew into the largest money transfer company serving the Somali diaspora and now operates in more than 120 countries, with headquarters in Dubai and more than 2,000 employees. Abdirashid Duale, who opened the company's first London branch in 1989, took over as chief executive from his father and has spread the group into banking, telecommunications, energy and real estate. Its holdings include Dahabshil Bank International, which opened in Djibouti in 2009, and a majority stake in Somali telecom operator Somtel, acquired in 2008. In 2023, the group opened the first phase of the Dahabshiil Oil Storage Terminal in the Somaliland port city of Berbera, a facility in which Dahabshiil and its partners have invested more than $100 million. somalia.content: Families fleeing Somalia crises find bleak prospects in Dadaab refugee camps - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Families fleeing Somalia crises find bleak prospects in Dadaab refugee camps Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday October 20, 2026 Nurto fled conflict in Baidoa and is struggling to support her seven children in Dadaab refugee camps/Ahmed Abdulahi/Ergo Families fleeing adversity in different parts of southern Somalia have been arriving in Kenya’s Dadaab refugee camps, where they find themselves with no means of making a living nor aid or support. They include families fleeing conflict in Baidoa, house demolitions by the Somali government in Mogadishu, and drought in their home areas. advertisements The new arrivals say they have received no reception support, shelter, or other forms of aid. Some are staying with relatives already struggling to make ends meet, while others have settled on their own on vacant land in Dadaab’s Ifo-2 camp. They lack food, housing, toilets and other basic services. Nurto Mohamed Ali, who arrived in Ifo-2 on 20 August, said her family had received no assistance and was struggling to meet basic needs. She is staying with relatives who arrived earlier. “Neighbours collect maize and cooking oil for us. That is how we are surviving now,” she said. “We have children who need food and bedding, but we have nothing to give them.” Nurto fled ongoing conflict in Baidoa between federal government forces and those loyal to the former South West State administration. She was a farmer raising her family on their two-hectare plot of land in Baidoa. Separated from her husband, she receives no support from him and is the sole income earner. In the refugee camp now, her seven children often go to bed hungry because she lacks food. They occupy a shelter made from plastic sheets, cloth and thorny branches in the yard of a relatives’ home – a household of 10. The days reach a scorching 37°C and the rainy season has begun. Nurto and her older children have to sleep outside without bedding while the youngest children cram themselves into the hut. Nurto said they had expected to receive assistance on arrival, including refugee registration cards, household items, and a house. She has received nothing. “We have no proper house, and even the people who arrived before us do not have one. The shelter situation is very difficult. We sleep on pieces of cloth and a small, broken mat,” she said. Other vulnerable new arrivals, including older people, people with disabilities, women and children, are finding no formal help in the camp, where some walk around daily asking more established residents for food. Hawo Mohamed Ali, her disabled husband, and their 10 children arrived in Ifo-2 on 1 August. They fled Mogadishu’s Hodan district after the government demolished their house, saying the land belonged to the state. They had lived in the house for 34 years without having formal land ownership documents. She said losing the home made it impossible for her family to remain in Mogadishu. “When we left and went outside, we found our land fenced off and surrounded by a wall,” she told Radio Ergo. “We were told the land would be measured and returned to us. Our houses were demolished using bulldozers, and we thought the land would be given back. Later, we were told it was government land and that we had to leave.” The demolition left Hawo’s family homeless and they decided their only option was to seek refuge in Dadaab. In Mogadishu, she earned a living selling meat and watermelon in local markets. In the refugee camp, however, they have not been registered and haven’t received aid cards or assistance. She looked for laundry work, but the jobs are irregular, so she has to ask others for help with food for her children. She lacks firewood and containers for collecting water. “The children’s father is disabled, and life is very difficult for us. My children are still young and have nothing here. We left our home and came to a place we do not know,” said Hawo, adding that the conditions in Dadaab were far worse than she had expected. The chairman of Hagardera camp, Khalif Dhubow Jelle, said the hardship facing new arrivals from Somalia had been brought to the attention of humanitarian agencies in the camps, but no effective response had followed. He recorded nearly 250 families having arrived from southern Somalia in the past three months. “Their living conditions are extremely poor. It is also the rainy season, yet these people have no shelter or place to stay. They are sitting in the open and have no food or water,” he said. The new arrivals are joining a refugee population already struggling with difficult living conditions because of reduced humanitarian aid and wider economic hardship across the camps. somalia.summary: Families fleeing crises in Somalia are facing dire conditions in the Dadaab refugee camps in Kenya. The camps, originally established to accommodate a temporary influx of refugees, are now home to over 200,000 people, leading to overcrowding and limited resources. Many refugees are struggling with inadequate access to food, clean water, and healthcare. The ongoing conflict, drought, and famine in Somalia have driven families to seek safety, but the camps offer little hope for a better future. Aid organizations are overwhelmed and unable to meet the growing needs of the population, leaving many refugees in a state of uncertainty and despair. The situation highlights the urgent need for international support and sustainable solutions to address the challenges faced by displaced families.

All nine cases belong to a single cluster linked to the first patient, a Kenyan national who travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda and died in Nairobi on October 5. According to the Ministry’s press release signed by Director General Dr. Patrick Amoth, all eight surviving patients are “improving and responding well to treatment” and are currently stable. Kenya has received 500 doses of medicines to support treatment, and 134 of 135 contacts (99.3 percent) have been traced and quarantined, well above the global benchmark of 85 percent. The Ministry also announced that contacts who entered quarantine on October 6 will complete their 21-day monitoring period and begin returning home from Saturday, October 25. “Having completed 21 days without symptoms, they pose no risk of infection to anyone,” the statement said. What Kenya’s Success Means for Somalia On its face, Kenya’s containment of the cluster is good news for Somalia. A uncontrolled outbreak in Nairobi, Somalia’s primary transit hub for international travel and humanitarian logistics, would have immediate and severe consequences for Mogadishu. The fact that all nine cases remain linked to a single chain, with no evidence of community transmission, suggests that Kenya’s contact tracing and quarantine measures have functioned as intended. But Kenya’s success also sharpens the contrast with Somalia’s own preparedness. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the earlier phase of the outbreak , Somalia’s Cabinet approved a national Ebola preparedness committee in early October, and health authorities deployed staff to Mogadishu airport to monitor arriving travelers. The government also quarantined ten citizens who returned from the DRC through Uganda, and a Somali citizen who had travelled with the Kenyan victim was placed in isolation at Forlanini Hospital in Mogadishu. The critical weakness remains at the points of entry. A 2024 baseline assessment conducted with WHO Somalia found that Somalia’s International Health Regulations core capacities at points of entry averaged 27 percent, with airports at only 20 percent. The assessment noted no dedicated isolation areas, no biosecure transport for suspected cases, and no standard operating procedures for disease detection at Somali airports. The Kenyan index patient transited through Uganda and flew to Nairobi without being detected at the airport. If a similar case were to arrive in Mogadishu, Somalia’s screening infrastructure would face the same test. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the initial quarantine measures , the Somali citizen who travelled with the Kenyan victim passed through Mogadishu airport’s standard health screening without raising concerns. The Regional Picture Kenya’s nine cases are part of a broader regional emergency. The Bundibugyo strain outbreak in the DRC has now surpassed 9,500 confirmed cases and more than 4,600 deaths, making it the second deadliest Ebola outbreak on record. The strain has no approved vaccine or specific treatment, though trials are underway. Nigeria confirmed an imported case in October, and the WHO has warned that the geographic spread of the outbreak is the widest in history. Kenya’s Health Ministry has distributed supplies to 12 very high-risk and 16 high-risk counties, established a dedicated laboratory at Kenyatta National Hospital to handle Ebola testing without contaminating the main lab, and trained nearly 5,000 healthcare workers. The WHO has provided $70,000 in essential medical supplies, including PPE and testing kits. Somalia has received support from IGAD and WHO, including a joint mission that developed a costed Ebola preparedness and response workplan, and a national simulation exercise in September 2026 that tested detection, verification, and response protocols. The exercise identified gaps in reporting lines, notification and referral pathways, point-of-entry arrangements, and public communication. Critical Note Kenya’s handling of its first Ebola outbreak has been competent and transparent. The Ministry of Health has published regular updates, traced nearly all contacts, and kept the public informed without inducing panic. The decision to allow quarantined contacts to return home after 21 days is scientifically sound and socially responsible. But Somalia should not mistake Kenya’s success for its own safety. The same qualities that have allowed Kenya to contain its cluster, a functioning health ministry with laboratory capacity, trained personnel, and a coherent command structure, are precisely those that Somalia lacks. The Kenyan index patient flew from Uganda to Nairobi and was not detected at the airport. A similar case arriving in Mogadishu would encounter screening systems that a WHO assessment rated at 20 percent capacity, with no dedicated isolation areas and no biosecure transport. The window for Somalia to close these gaps is narrowing. Kenya’s cluster appears contained, but the DRC outbreak continues to accelerate, and the movement of people across East Africa is constant. The Somali government has established a preparedness committee and deployed staff to airports. Those are necessary first steps. They are not sufficient. The difference between Kenya and Somalia in this outbreak is not luck. It is institutional capacity. Until Somalia builds that capacity, its border defenses will remain a promise rather than a barrier. Share your story. The swearing-in follows the certification of the September 30 parliamentary election results by Somalia’s Supreme Court, which confirmed the Justice and Solidarity Party (JSP) secured 78 of the 99 seats in the assembly. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the electoral timetable , the court stated that no legal challenges had been filed against the results, clearing the way for the new legislature to convene. According to the schedule published by the National Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (NIEBC), candidates for Speaker and Deputy Speakers submitted their applications on Wednesday, October 21. Campaign speeches and the speakership vote are scheduled for Thursday, October 22. The timeline then shifts to the executive. Applications for the regional presidency and vice-presidency will open on Friday, October 23, with candidate speeches and the final vote set for Saturday, October 24. A Parliament of Unprecedented Composition The September 30 vote marked the first time residents of Hirshabelle directly elected both regional lawmakers and local councillors, replacing the previous system of indirect clan-based selection. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the election results , 114,633 people cast ballots across 10 districts, with 112,466 votes declared valid. The JSP’s victory was overwhelming. The party received more than 88,000 votes, giving it nearly four-fifths of the seats in the new assembly. Karaama finished second with six seats, followed by Iftiin Qaran with five and Sincad with three. In the simultaneous local council elections, JSP won 158 of the 222 seats contested, further consolidating its control over Hirshabelle’s political institutions. The Unresolved Hiiraan Question While the procedural path to a new administration is clear, the political foundation remains contested. The JSP has nominated incumbent President Ali Abdullahi Hussein Guudlaawe for another term, a decision that has sharpened a long-running power-sharing dispute between the Hawadle community of Hiiraan and the Abgaal community of Middle Shabelle. Hirshabelle Vice President Yusuf Ahmed Hagar Dabageed, a Hawadle politician, has publicly accused President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud of reneging on a promise to return the regional presidency to the Hawadle clan. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the JSP nomination dispute , Dabageed stated that when he asked the president about his own candidacy, the president replied that he would give the position to Guudlaawe instead. The dispute has also raised questions about the inclusivity of the electoral process in Hiiraan. Prior to the parliamentary vote, Dabageed warned that elections could not proceed in the region without a political agreement involving traditional elders and local stakeholders. While voting did take place in Beledweyne, the underlying grievances remain unresolved. As reported in FTL Somalia’s analysis of the Hawadle political crisis , the community’s sense of abandonment has pushed some leaders toward dangerous alternatives, including reported contacts with Al-Shabaab . The JSP has selected former Hiiraan governor Abdifatah Hassan Afrah as its vice-presidential candidate, pairing him with Guudlaawe in the forthcoming leadership election. The arrangement is intended to balance the ticket, but it does not address the Hawadle demand for the presidency itself. Critical Note The swearing-in of Hirshabelle’s new parliament is a procedural milestone, and the direct election of lawmakers represents a genuine shift from the indirect selection systems that have governed Somali regional politics for years. The JSP’s victory is decisive, and the party now controls the institutions through which Hirshabelle’s next leadership will be chosen. But the parliament that convened in Jowhar on Tuesday does not represent a political consensus. It represents the outcome of an election that the JSP dominated, in a state where the ruling party at the federal level has openly backed its preferred candidates for regional office. The Hawadle community’s demand for the presidency, articulated by the regional vice president and supported by traditional elders, has not been resolved. It has been overruled by the arithmetic of the JSP’s 78-seat majority. Guudlaawe will almost certainly be re-elected on Saturday. The question is whether his new mandate will be seen as legitimate by the constituencies that feel excluded from the process. A parliament elected directly is a step forward. A presidency elected by a parliament that was itself the product of a lopsided contest is a different matter. The next five days will produce a government. They will not, by themselves, produce the political trust that Hirshabelle has lacked since its formation.
